raw_text:
### Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the management of severe aortic stenosis. While transfemoral (TF) arterial access remains the gold-standard route, severe peripheral artery disease, vessel tortuosity, heavy calcification, or small minimal lumen diameters preclude a TF approach in 5% to 15% of candidates. In these patients, alternative access options are necessary. Historically, surgical transapical or transaortic pathways were employed, but they carry considerable thoracotomy-related morbidity and mortality. Newer extrathoracic arterial access strategies, such as transaxillary/subclavian and transcarotid approaches, are less invasive but still present risks of stroke, local nerve injury, and usually require surgical exposure under general anesthesia. 

To overcome these limitations, a fully percutaneous, non-thoracic approach was conceptualized: transcaval (cavo-aortic) access. First validated in preclinical models [1] and translated into human practice in 2013 [2], transcaval access enables the delivery of large-bore sheaths into the abdominal aorta by crossing from the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC). By utilizing a completely percutaneous venous entry, the technique preserves the minimalist procedural benefits of TAVR while bypassing diseased iliofemoral arteries [3-5]. Comparative registry analyses have demonstrated that transcaval access offers favorable short-term outcomes compared to more invasive open surgical access routes [6].

### Physiology and Preprocedural Planning
The physiological safety of transcaval access is inherently counterintuitive but mathematically robust. When a large-bore tract is created between the infrarenal abdominal aorta and the adjacent IVC, retroperitoneal hemorrhage is prevented because the surrounding retroperitoneal space is not surgically opened and quickly pressurizes. Once the local hydrostatic pressure of the retroperitoneal space exceeds the low venous pressure of the IVC, any aortic bleeding decompressively shunts directly into the IVC rather than extravasating catastrophically into the retroperitoneum [7]. 

Successful execution demands meticulous preprocedural planning using multi-detector computed tomography (CT) [8]. Imaging is used to identify a calcium-free "landing zone" on the abdominal aorta where it directly abuts the IVC, ensuring a crossing trajectory that avoids major collateral branches or intervascular bowel loops. This crossing is achieved utilizing transcatheter electrosurgery [9]. Typically, a microcatheter and a standard guidewire energized with radiofrequency energy are used to puncture from the IVC, across the retroperitoneal space, and into a snare prepositioned in the abdominal aorta. Alternative crossing methods, such as laser-assisted access, have also been described [10]. Remarkably, transcaval access can be successfully performed even in highly complex anatomical settings, such as across synthetic aortic polyester grafts [11], thrombosed aneurysms [12], or previously implanted aortic endografts [13].

### Procedural Efficacy, Closure, and Clinical Evidence
Once cavo-aortic crossing is achieved, a stiff guidewire is positioned, allowing the large-bore TAVR introducer sheath to be advanced from the femoral vein into the abdominal aorta. The structural intervention is then completed in standard fashion. At the procedure's conclusion, the tract is percutaneously closed using an off-label nitinol cardiac occluder device, such as an Amplatzer duct occluder or muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD) occluder [14]. Long-term follow-up demonstrates that these tracts heal safely; the majority of residual aortocaval fistulas spontaneously close within days to months, with negligible rates of delayed complications or device failure [15]. To simplify closure and eliminate the need for off-label implants, purpose-built transcaval closure devices have undergone successful clinical testing [16].

Robust clinical registry and meta-analysis data support the safety of transcaval TAVR [17]. A multicenter European registry [18] and institutional cohort studies [19,20] have shown technical success rates exceeding 98%, with low rates of stroke, acute kidney injury, and procedural mortality. When compared to the transaxillary approach, propensity-weighted analyses from the STS/ACC TVT registry show a fivefold lower risk of stroke and transient ischemic attacks in transcaval patients, presumably due to the avoidance of head and neck vessel manipulation [21,22], with outcomes adjudicated under standardized VARC-3 criteria [23]. Contemporary best-practice consensus documents have standardized the technique, highlighting its reproducibility across diverse structural heart programs [24].

### Beyond TAVR: Expanding Horizons
While developed primarily for TAVR, the applications of transcaval access have expanded to other complex endovascular and circulatory support procedures. It has been successfully utilized to deliver large-bore thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) grafts in patients with prohibitive iliofemoral conduits [25]. Crucially, in cardiogenic shock, transcaval access allows the percutaneous delivery of high-flow mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices. For example, it enables the delivery of the Impella 5.0 or 5.5 microaxial pumps [26], facilitates transcaval left atrial veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) [27], and permits completely venous biventricular MCS configurations [28]. Propensity studies show that these transcaval approaches compare favorably to subclavian surgical cutdowns in critically ill cohorts [29].

### Conclusion
Transcaval access is a versatile, fully percutaneous alternative for structural heart and large-bore endovascular interventions [30]. By leveraging unique retroperitoneal physiology and advanced electrosurgery, it bypasses hostile peripheral arterial anatomy, mitigates the risk of stroke associated with supra-aortic access, and avoids the morbidity of surgical thoracoabdominal conduits. Ongoing refinements in dedicated closure technology will further solidify transcaval access as a vital component of the structural heart team’s armamentarium.
